items.title: Huawei Details Xingji Positioning: Lane-Level Fixes in Tunnels, Floor Detection in Parking Garages
items.summary: Huawei details its new Xingji Positioning stack, which uses AI speed estimation and 3D road matching alongside other technologies to provide highly accurate, lane-level positioning in complex environments.

items.title: DeepSeek’s cost-saving AI may lead to inaccuracy in model performance: research - South China Morning Post
items.summary: Research suggests that DeepSeek's cost-saving AI approach may lead to inaccuracies in its model performance, highlighting findings about AI model trade-offs.

items.title: Faithfulness Without Anchors: A Position Paper on the Structural Misalignments of Explainable AI Faithfulness Metrics for Feature Importance
items.summary: A position paper discusses the structural misalignments of faithfulness metrics used in Explainable AI (XAI) for feature importance, arguing that current methods fail to increase trust.

items.title: EliteTable: Self-Improving Program Search for Executable Control Policies
items.summary: EliteTable introduces a self-improving program-search algorithm guided by large language models for generating executable control policies, evaluated across Gymnasium control tasks.

items.title: Equal-Budget Monte Carlo Tree Search versus Randomized-Restart List Scheduling for DAG Workflows: A Controlled Equal-Budget Computational Study
items.summary: A computational study compares Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) with randomized-restart list scheduling for Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) workflows, evaluating methods under equal search effort.

items.title: Know What You Don't Know: Agentic Data Synthesis by Evolving Generation Space for Closed-Loop Learning
items.summary: A research paper proposes a method for 'Agentic Data Synthesis' that involves evolving the generation space for closed-loop learning to improve interactive AI agents' experience.

items.title: Beyond Binary Verifiable Rewards: Behavioral Self-Rewarding for SWE Agents
items.summary: A study explores 'Behavioral Self-Rewarding' for software engineering (SWE) agents, aiming to improve upon binary verifiable rewards by allowing policies to judge their own debugging quality.

items.title: CLEAT: Learning Value-Guided Clarification for Interactive Agents
items.summary: CLEAT proposes a method for 'Learning Value-Guided Clarification' to improve interactive LLM agents by helping them align actions with users' unstated goals and constraints.

items.title: MagicBeanStalk: Escaping the RLVR Zero Advantage Trap with Recursive Data Synthesis
items.summary: MagicBeanStalk introduces 'Recursive Data Synthesis' to guide the generation of effective Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) data, addressing challenges in data-centric scaling.

items.title: Faithful and Complete LLM-Assisted Automated Construction of Hierarchical Hardware Knowledge Graphs
items.summary: Research describes an LLM-assisted automated method for constructing hierarchical hardware knowledge graphs from datasheets, aiming to improve hardware compatibility verification.

items.title: Representation Alignment from a Few Paired Data via Distilled Optimal Transport
items.summary: A new method using 'Distilled Optimal Transport' is proposed for representation alignment between unimodal encoders, effective even with only a few paired data examples.

items.title: EvoBelief: Falsifiable World Models for Self-Improving LLM Agents
items.summary: EvoBelief explores the concept of 'Falsifiable World Models' for self-improving LLM agents, focusing on evolving their beliefs about environment dynamics for better performance.

items.title: VEPA: Verified Evolving Formal Policy for Lifelong LLM Agent Guardrails
items.summary: VEPA presents a method for 'Verified Evolving Formal Policy' to create lifelong LLM agent guardrails, ensuring inspectable and deterministic decisions for safety and security.

items.title: Reward Hacking as a Transmissible Strategy in Multi-Agent Coding Systems
items.summary: A study investigates 'Reward Hacking' as a transmissible strategy within multi-agent coding systems, where agents bypass evaluation to gain rewards without genuine solutions.

items.title: Neural networks are more modular than single neurons suggest
items.summary: A research paper challenges the view that neural networks lack modular organization, proposing a nested hierarchy of modularity that suggests they are more modular than previously thought.

items.title: Towards Defining, Measuring, and Leveraging Creativity in AI Applications
items.summary: A paper discusses the challenges in defining, measuring, and leveraging creativity in AI applications, emphasizing the need for a conceptually grounded and empirically applicable formal definition.

items.title: Mitigating Capability Degradation in LLM Self-Improvement via Representation Geometry Regularization
items.summary: Research introduces a method called 'Representation Geometry Regularization' to mitigate capability degradation in LLM self-improvement processes using On-Policy Self-distillation.

items.title: Collaborative Theory of Mind: Learning to Self-Revise by Anticipating User Responses
items.summary: This paper introduces a framework for large language models to self-revise and improve collaboration in multi-turn interactions by anticipating user responses. It addresses LLMs' struggle to adapt and revise assumptions based on user feedback.

items.title: OGPO: Offline Goal-conditioned Policy Optimization for Recoverable Vision-Language-Action Models
items.summary: This paper proposes OGPO (Offline Goal-conditioned Policy Optimization), a new method for training Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models to improve robotic manipulation beyond trajectory-level supervised imitation.

items.title: AI-Mediation in Retail Markets: Revenue Effects and Assortment Optimization
items.summary: This study analyzes the revenue effects and assortment optimization strategies for retailers when AI shopping assistants mediate product choices for consumers.

items.title: Collaborative Learning and Reasoning over Model Slices
items.summary: This paper explores collaborative learning and reasoning over "model slices" to mitigate error propagation in large language models, aiming to improve their overall reasoning capabilities.

items.title: Learning More by Training Less: Uncertainty-Guided Progressive Contraction for Efficient Reasoning Post-Training
items.summary: This study introduces "Uncertainty-Guided Progressive Contraction" as a method for achieving more efficient reasoning in large language models post-training, aiming to reduce training costs without sacrificing performance.

items.title: Beyond Semantic IDs: Finite-Beam Reachability and Continuous-Query Generation in Generative Recommendation
items.summary: This work explores limitations of Semantic ID decoding in generative recommendation systems and investigates continuous-query generation to improve the reachability of items in returned lists.

items.title: Provenance-Aware Belief Updating in Human-AI Feedback Loops
items.summary: This study investigates provenance-aware belief updating in human-AI feedback loops, examining whether language models can use report lineage to accurately update beliefs based on evidence origin and avoid treating repeated information as independent corroboration.

items.title: Does Location Matter? A Black-Box Causal Audit Reveals Model-Dependent Audio Grounding in LALM Hallucination
items.summary: This paper presents a black-box causal audit revealing model-dependent audio grounding in Large Audio-Language Model (LALM) hallucination, investigating how LALMs affirm absent sounds and evaluating a mitigation strategy.

items.title: Looking Ahead and Back: Anticipatory Generative Modeling for Road-Network Trajectories
items.summary: This research explores anticipatory generative modeling for road-network trajectories to enhance urban applications like traffic management and urban planning, focusing on critical transitions at intersections.

items.title: VIGOR: Verifiable Industrial Geometry Optimization and Repair in Scene Programs
items.summary: This item presents 'VIGOR,' a system for verifiable industrial geometry optimization and repair in scene programs generated by LLMs, ensuring engineering feasibility beyond mere executability.

items.title: AdaC-GRPO: Towards Mastering Long-Horizon Visual Sudoku Puzzles via Adaptive Curriculum Learning
items.summary: This research introduces 'AdaC-GRPO,' a method for mastering long-horizon visual Sudoku puzzles through adaptive curriculum learning, enhancing reasoning in large language models via reinforcement learning.

items.title: BoundaryEvo: Data-Model Co-Evolution at the Capability Boundary for Long-Chain Reasoning Distillation
items.summary: This paper presents 'BoundaryEvo,' a data-model co-evolution approach for long-chain reasoning distillation, designed to improve the reasoning ability of small language models by adaptively selecting useful examples.

items.title: RegulaTutor: A Theory-Informed Framework for Long-Term Personalized Learning
items.summary: This research proposes 'RegulaTutor,' a theory-informed framework for long-term personalized learning that utilizes language models to translate a learner's history into appropriate instructional support.

items.title: CircuitTree: Composing Circuits into A Syllable Transcriber
items.summary: CircuitTree proposes a practical method for composing modular, interpretable subnetworks ('circuits') discovered within a monolithic neural network into a single model, demonstrating its application as a syllable transcriber. The goal is to improve neural network interpretability by decomposing tasks into identifiable subtasks.

items.title: Behind-the-Meter Photovoltaic Visibility from Net Smart Meters: Deployment Regimes and Operational Insights
items.summary: This research explores using deep-learning-based photovoltaic (PV) disaggregation from net smart meters to provide distribution operators with visibility into behind-the-meter PV generation. It evaluates the operational value of this AI application under different deployment regimes.

items.title: GlucoPRISM: Protocol-Supervised Pretraining for Cross-Cohort Glucose Transfer
items.summary: GlucoPRISM investigates protocol-supervised pretraining for continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) foundation models to improve cross-cohort glucose transfer. The method aims to better separate individual, daily event, and sensor measurement information in the encoded representations.

items.title: Market Impact Estimation via Causal Foundation Models
items.summary: This research proposes using causal foundation models for market impact estimation in financial trading, addressing the challenge of distinguishing actual price changes from what would have happened without a trade. It highlights the causal nature of market impact compared to classical regression models.

items.title: Efficient Learning of Survival Analysis Models Under Outcome-Dependent Truncation and Censoring
items.summary: This paper focuses on efficient learning for survival analysis models under conditions of outcome-dependent truncation and censoring, where training data may not be representative of future predictive tasks. It addresses challenges arising from biases in practical datasets for machine learning.

items.title: Enriched Holomorphic Neural Networks for 2D and 3D Laplace Problems
items.summary: This research introduces enriched holomorphic neural networks designed to solve 2D and 3D Laplace boundary-value problems, particularly where singular behavior occurs. The approach combines neural networks with singular functions to better resolve complex geometries.

items.title: Sample-Adaptive Zeroth-Order Post-Training
items.summary: This research proposes a sample-adaptive zeroth-order (ZO) post-training method for fine-tuning large language models, aiming to improve efficiency and reduce estimation variance. The method addresses limitations of existing ZO optimization techniques that sample training examples uniformly.

items.title: An all-transistor physical-learning transformer can be trained to perform in-context learning
items.summary: This research demonstrates that an all-transistor physical-learning transformer can be trained to perform in-context learning, distinguishing it from traditional perceptron-based systems. It highlights a novel hardware-software co-design approach for AI learning.

items.title: Realism VS Accuracy: Event Sequence Forecasting from a Generative Modeling Perspective
items.summary: This research investigates event sequence forecasting from a generative modeling perspective, analyzing the trade-off between realism and accuracy in predicting multi-horizon event sequences. It focuses on event chains with heterogeneous features relevant to various fields like finance and healthcare.

items.title: Machine Learning and Time-Series Foundation Models for Day-Ahead Electricity Forecasting in a University Building
items.summary: This research applies and benchmarks machine learning and time-series foundation models for day-ahead electricity forecasting in a university building. The goal is to assist building operators in scheduling services based on anticipated energy demand, considering model accuracy and computational requirements.

items.title: Amortised Inference through One-Step Implicit Sampling
items.summary: This research introduces a method for amortized inference through one-step implicit sampling, aiming to improve the efficiency of drawing unbiased samples from high-dimensional Bayesian posterior distributions. It addresses the challenges of multi-step sampling processes in existing algorithms.

items.title: Expert-level detection of low-voltage intervals in EEG as a robust biomarker of neonatal encephalopathy
items.summary: This research focuses on expert-level AI detection of low-voltage intervals in neonatal EEG as a robust biomarker for neonatal encephalopathy. It addresses the challenge of translating visual discontinuity markers like inter-burst intervals into quantifiable AI detection methods.

items.title: A Categorical Atlas of Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning: Cones, Orbits, and Gauges
items.summary: This research paper presents a categorical atlas to compare hundreds of parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods, treating them as maps in weight space.

items.title: Kernelized Parameter Sensitivity Atlases for Amortized Conditional Interpretability
items.summary: This paper derives Kernelized Parameter Sensitivity Atlases (KPSA) as a new method for amortized conditional interpretability, aiming to provide input-specific information about model parameters more efficiently than gradient-based attribution.

items.title: KITE: A Knowledge-Injected Temporal Encoder for Time-Series Event Forecasting
items.summary: This paper introduces KITE, a Knowledge-Injected Temporal Encoder designed for forecasting rare, high-cost events in multivariate time-series systems by incorporating expert knowledge.

items.title: Neural expectation-maximization and meta-models
items.summary: This paper reinterprets Transformer networks as learned approximations to a hybrid probabilistic-inference procedure that combines max-product Loopy Belief Propagation with Expectation-Maximization in partially observed Markov Random Fields.

items.title: Static Gradient Attribution Underperforms a Density-Matched Random Mask on Loss-Based Forgetting Within LoRA B-Matrix
items.summary: This research finds that static gradient attribution underperforms a density-matched random mask for preventing loss-based forgetting within the LoRA B-Matrix in parameter-efficient continual learning.

items.title: NV-Tesseract-AD: Curriculum-Enhanced Conditional Diffusion for Multivariate Time-Series Anomaly Detection
items.summary: This paper proposes NV-Tesseract-AD, a curriculum learning-enhanced conditional diffusion framework for multivariate time-series anomaly detection.

items.title: REDaCT: Collapse-Free Unlearning in Large Reasoning Models
items.summary: This paper introduces REDaCT, a new method for collapse-free unlearning in large reasoning models, enabling the removal of specific information from reasoning traces and final answers without degrading model coherence.

items.title: Coordinate-Free Automatic Differentiation
items.summary: This paper proposes a new coordinate-free approach to automatic differentiation, addressing limitations of current frameworks that implicitly fix a basis of Euclidean space for defining gradients and Jacobians.

items.title: Meta-Reflective Evolution Effectively Improves Production AI Systems
items.summary: This paper introduces Meta-Reflective Evolution, an LLM-guided evolutionary optimization method that effectively improves production AI systems by addressing the limitations of existing optimization approaches.

items.title: The Expressive Power of Random-Feature MPNNs Across Graph Sizes
items.summary: This paper analyzes the expressive power of random-feature Message-Passing Neural Networks (MPNNs) across different graph sizes, addressing limitations in existing theoretical analyses.

items.title: Inverse Synthesis of Shock Time Series from Shock Response Spectra Using Ensembles of Conditional Variational Autoencoders
items.summary: This paper proposes using ensembles of Conditional Variational Autoencoders for the inverse synthesis of shock time series from shock response spectra.

items.title: Cross-Behavior Policy Optimization: Unified Learning from Offline Demonstrations and On- and Off-Policy Rollouts via a Shared Regression Target
items.summary: This paper proposes Cross-Behavior Policy Optimization, a unified method for learning from offline demonstrations and on- and off-policy rollouts using a shared regression target, improving reasoning post-training.

items.title: When Generative Models Act as Simulators
items.summary: This paper investigates the conditions under which a generative model can effectively act as a simulator, exploring their capacity to represent and allow editing of environmental states.

items.title: Reinforcement Learning via Fixed-point Flow Matching
items.summary: This paper proposes a new method for reinforcement learning called Fixed-point Flow Matching, which addresses the challenge of generating samples from complex, multimodal optimal policy distributions.

items.title: Robust Langevin Sampling under State-Dependent Heavy-Tailed Noise with Applications to LLM Fine-Tuning
items.summary: This paper presents a method for robust Langevin sampling under state-dependent heavy-tailed noise, addressing limitations in existing convergence guarantees with applications to LLM fine-tuning.

items.title: Personalized Federated Direct Preference Optimization via LoRA Adapters
items.summary: This paper introduces Federated Direct Preference Optimization (FedDPO), a method enabling privacy-preserving alignment of language models across distributed agents without centralizing sensitive preference data, addressing limitations of existing FedDPO analysis.

items.title: GIST: Generator-state-Informed Supervision for Tabular Foundation Models
items.summary: This paper proposes GIST (Generator-state-Informed Supervision), a new method for training tabular foundation models that uses intermediate generator states to reveal label uncertainty, improving pretraining beyond sampled hard query labels.

items.title: Controlled-Minimax: Stabilizing Adversarial Optimization via Control Theory
items.summary: This research investigates stability issues in minimax optimization, fundamental to adversarial learning, by modeling training dynamics as continuous-time dynamical systems and proposes a control theory-based approach to stabilize it.

items.title: Diffusion Precipitation Generation with Medium-range Weather Forecasting
items.summary: This paper proposes using diffusion models to generate daily precipitation forecasts, aiming to improve accuracy by addressing regional and intensity-dependent biases found in weather foundation models trained on reanalysis data.

items.title: Evidential Multimodal Transformers with Dempster-Shafer Fusion for Emotion Recognition
items.summary: This paper presents an Evidential Multimodal Transformer with Dempster-Shafer Fusion for emotion recognition, which robustly handles corrupted or contradictory sensor data by assigning lower confidence in uncertain situations, unlike traditional softmax methods.

items.title: Generalized Proximal Policy Optimization: Unifying LLM RL Algorithms from the Perspective of Divergence
items.summary: This paper introduces Generalized Proximal Policy Optimization, a new framework that unifies existing LLM reinforcement learning algorithms and improves upon the dominant PPO approach by allowing adaptive resistance to policy shifts.

items.title: Trajectory-Aware Policy Optimization: Closing the State Distribution Gap in Long-Horizon LLM RL
items.summary: This paper proposes Trajectory-Aware Policy Optimization to address the state distribution gap in long-horizon LLM reinforcement learning, mitigating the issue where local policy mismatches compound over autoregressive rollouts.

items.title: AutoIndexer: Flexible-Order Decoding by Training Causal Models on Chains of Edits
items.summary: This paper introduces AutoIndexer, a method for flexible-order decoding that trains causal models on chains of edits, offering an alternative to traditional autoregressive decoding which struggles with non-causally ordered data.

items.title: Contextual Correction of Parallel Draftsfor Speculative Decoding
items.summary: This paper proposes a technique for contextual correction of parallel drafts to enhance speculative decoding, a method that accelerates large language model inference by verifying multiple proposed tokens in parallel.

items.title: One Model to Loop Them All: Elastic Latent Recurrence for Language Models
items.summary: This paper proposes Elastic Latent Recurrence for language models, a method allowing a single model checkpoint to trade inference compute for accuracy by repeatedly applying a shared layer block, addressing the 'one-loop tax'.

items.title: Self-Preservation in Language Models
items.summary: This paper explores 'Self-Preservation' in language models, where models generate supplementary tasks to preserve prior capabilities during continual learning, helping to mitigate forgetting beyond explicitly provided task data.

items.title: Activating the Annotator: Operationalising Lived Experience in Data Annotation
items.summary: This research explores methods for operationalizing annotator positionality, or lived experience, in data annotation for subjective NLP tasks, moving beyond static demographic attributes to improve label accuracy.

items.title: Forecasting Corpus-Sampling Disagreement in Masked Text Reconstruction
items.summary: This research investigates how a predictor's outputs for masked text reconstruction change when using different corpus samples, evaluating it on GPT-2 vocabulary.

items.title: CliQ-RRG: Clinical-Knowledge Guided Disease-aware Visual-Textual Alignment for QA-Style Radiology Report Generation
items.summary: This paper presents CliQ-RRG, a system that uses clinical knowledge for disease-aware visual-textual alignment to automatically generate QA-style radiology reports.

items.title: BenCoDiC: A Large-Scale Contextual Cyberbullying Corpus for Bengali Political News Discourse FULL VERSION
items.summary: This paper introduces BenCoDiC, a large-scale contextual corpus for detecting cyberbullying in Bengali political news discourse, addressing limitations in existing datasets. It aims to improve robust detection and comprehensive study of harasser behaviors in online communities.

items.title: SOAR: Source-Aware Reinforcement Learning with Precise Credit Assignment for Search Agents
items.summary: SOAR is a new method for Source-Aware Reinforcement Learning with precise credit assignment, designed to prevent evidence fabrication in search agents. It addresses the issue of agents over-relying on unreliable internal knowledge instead of external information.

items.title: PreSTO: Predictive Subtree Prefetching for Fast LLM Power Sampling
items.summary: PreSTO (Predictive Subtree Prefetching) is a technique designed to speed up LLM power sampling, which is used to improve LLM reasoning at test time. It addresses the sequential nature of PowerMH updates to make the sampling process faster.

items.title: SharP: Soft and Hard Prompt-Guided Augmentation with LLM for Low Resource Fake News Detection
items.summary: SharP introduces a method for soft and hard prompt-guided augmentation using LLMs to improve fake news detection in low-resource conditions. It addresses challenges posed by scarce labeled data in this domain.

items.title: Agreement Without Alignment: Label-Free Rubric Clarification Increases LLM-Judge Consensus but Not Agreement with Humans
items.summary: This research proposes a label-free procedure to clarify rubrics for LLM judges, which increases consensus among them but does not necessarily improve agreement with human evaluations. It aims to address disagreements in LLM-based evaluation panels.

items.title: Host-Aware Web Crawling for LLM Pretraining Data
items.summary: This research investigates host-aware web crawling strategies to optimize the collection of high-quality pretraining data for large language models. It aims to improve data selection pipelines by efficiently allocating crawling budgets across and within hosts.

items.title: Overcoming Data Imbalances with Expert Selection Biases
items.summary: This research explores overcoming data imbalances in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models for LLMs through expert selection biases. It aims to improve expert specialization during pretraining, particularly when data is imbalanced.

items.title: MoPrO-SD: Modular Prompt Optimization for Stance Detection
items.summary: MoPrO-SD introduces Modular Prompt Optimization for stance detection using large language models, addressing challenges posed by implicit opinions and sarcasm. This technique offers an alternative to fine-tuning for improving LLM performance on this task.

items.title: Towards the Roof of the World: NLP Progress in Tibetan Languages
items.summary: This paper presents the first systematic bibliometric survey of Natural Language Processing (NLP) progress in Tibetan languages. It reviews 140 publications from 2004 to 2026, highlighting the underrepresentation of Tibetan in NLP.

items.title: zip2zip++: Towards Inference-Time Token Compression with Minimal Quality Loss
items.summary: zip2zip++ introduces a method for inference-time token compression for language models using dynamic vocabularies, aiming for minimal quality loss. It demonstrates that efficiency gains from compression do not necessarily come at a fundamental cost to reasoning and perplexity.

items.title: Training User Simulators with Latent Intrinsic Feedback
items.summary: This research explores training user simulators with latent intrinsic feedback to develop LLM assistants capable of handling nuanced multi-turn conversations. It focuses on leveraging user simulation as a direct source of feedback for assistant training.

items.title: Multi-Stream Attention Residuals
items.summary: This research introduces Multi-Stream Attention Residuals (MSAR), an extension of Attention Residuals (AttnRes), which enables content-dependent retrieval over network depth by treating it as multi-head attention along the depth axis.

items.title: TraceICL: Thread-Resolved Demonstration Curation with Consistency Calibration for Robust Multimodal In-Context Learning
items.summary: This research proposes TraceICL, a method for thread-resolved demonstration curation with consistency calibration, aiming to improve the robustness of multimodal in-context learning for large vision-language models.

items.title: MIRAGE: Metric Inference and Reliability-Aware Gaussian Estimation from Feed-Forward Vision
items.summary: MIRAGE is a method for metric inference and reliability-aware Gaussian estimation from feed-forward vision, aiming to combine high-quality image-stream reconstruction with the metrically accurate motion of LiDAR-inertial estimation.

items.title: Scaling Multi-Teacher Distillation for Digital Pathology
items.summary: This paper investigates scaling multi-teacher distillation, a method for transferring knowledge from multiple teacher networks to a single student network, with a focus on its application and challenges in digital pathology.

items.title: MemReg: Streaming Outdoor LiDAR Point Cloud Registration with Hybrid Memory Buffers
items.summary: MemReg is a novel multi-frame network proposed for streaming outdoor LiDAR point cloud registration, which utilizes hybrid memory buffers to account for temporal correlations within streaming sequences.

items.title: Shift-Aware Identity-Guided Latent Refinement for Referring Audio--Visual Segmentation
items.summary: This paper proposes Shift-Aware Identity-Guided Latent Refinement, a method for Referring Audio-Visual Segmentation (Ref-AVS), an emergent multimodal task requiring precise object identification based on both visual and auditory cues.

items.title: Domain Adaptation of SAM 2.1 for Building-Component Segmentation in Image-Based 3D Reconstruction
items.summary: This research focuses on domain adaptation of the Segment Anything Model (SAM 2.1) for building-component segmentation, a crucial step in image-based 3D reconstruction workflows.

items.title: Spend Where It Matters: Particle Search with MH Refinement for Budget-Constrained Audio-Visual Alignment
items.summary: This paper introduces a method using particle search with MH refinement for budget-constrained audio-visual alignment, aiming to optimize joint audio-visual generation under limited computational resources.

items.title: Selective Spatio-Temporal Fruit Inspector (S$^2$FI): A Mamba-based Framework for Rotational Fruit Quality Assessment
items.summary: This paper presents S$^2$FI (Selective Spatio-Temporal Fruit Inspector), a Mamba-based framework developed for rotational fruit quality assessment to address challenges in post-harvest sorting for the fruit and vegetable industry.

items.title: ROSETTA: Rotation Subspace Estimation for Training-free Transmodal Alignment
items.summary: ROSETTA introduces a method for Rotation Subspace Estimation to achieve training-free transmodal alignment, enabling accurate matching of queries against databases built with different sensors or processed by distinct encoders.

items.title: MeshBind: Point-to-Mesh Binding for Non-Rigid Scene Flow Automatic Annotation
items.summary: This paper introduces MeshBind, an automatic annotation method that uses mesh models to generate per-point scene flow for non-rigid objects, crucial for autonomous driving and robotic applications.

items.title: AD-SRF: Attack-Defense Semantic Reinforcement for Multi-Modal Image Fusion
items.summary: This research proposes AD-SRF, an attack-defense semantic reinforcement framework for multi-modal image fusion, aiming to better balance visual quality and semantic attributes.

items.title: A Lightweight Velocity Correction Framework for Improving Instruction Following in Few-Step Text-to-Image Generation
items.summary: This work presents a lightweight velocity correction framework to improve instruction following in few-step text-to-image generation, particularly for complex prompts, without altering generator parameters.

items.title: JMT-YOLO: Multi-task Domain Adaptation via Segmentation-Guided Consistency Learning
items.summary: This paper introduces JMT-YOLO, a multi-task domain adaptation method that uses segmentation-guided consistency learning to enhance object detection performance across different datasets.

items.title: BLEND: Balancing Personalization vs. Generalization in Federated Vision-Language Models
items.summary: This research introduces BLEND, a new framework designed to jointly enhance personalization and generalization in federated vision-language models by integrating federated learning within VLM fine-tuning.

items.title: What Egocentric Video Embeddings Encode and How to Combine Them with Inertial Sensors for Human Activity Recognition
items.summary: This study investigates what egocentric video embeddings encode and how to effectively combine them with body-worn inertial sensors for improved human activity recognition.

items.title: UniDeblur: Unified Motion Deblurring via Fourier Convolution Learning
items.summary: This paper proposes UniDeblur, a unified motion deblurring method utilizing Fourier convolution learning to improve performance across various scenarios, cameras, and image contents.

items.title: In-Context Learning Can Help Vision-Language Models Overcome Training Priors
items.summary: This research demonstrates that in-context learning can help vision-language models overcome strong training priors, enabling them to better respond to visual evidence that violates those regularities.

items.title: Video Codec-Guided Training-Free Token Compression for Video Large Language Models
items.summary: This work introduces a video codec-guided, training-free token compression method for Video Large Language Models (VLLMs) to achieve more efficient inference by reducing visual token sequences.

items.title: MotionCoach: Constructing Multimodal Guidance for Video Professional Motion Editing
items.summary: This paper introduces MotionCoach, a method for constructing multimodal guidance specifically for professional motion editing in videos, building upon existing video editing models.

items.title: Learning Representations to Guide Pixel Diffusion Transformers
items.summary: This research investigates visual representations for pixel diffusion transformers, uncovering insights into what makes them useful for guiding generative quality in image creation.

items.title: The Evidence Anchoring Boundary: Where Visual Interventions Matter and When They Help in Multimodal LLMs
items.summary: This study investigates the 'Evidence Anchoring Boundary' to understand where and when visual interventions are effective in reducing hallucinations in multimodal large language models.

items.title: Learning Features, Not Layouts: Feature-Axis Attention as a Transfer Prior for Medical Imaging
items.summary: This research proposes Feature-Axis Attention as a transfer prior for medical imaging, addressing the unreliability of natural-image-pretrained foundation models under domain shifts and label scarcity.

items.title: Unified Generative Video Compression with Autoregressive and Bidirectional Video Diffusion
items.summary: This work presents a unified generative video compression method utilizing both autoregressive and bidirectional video diffusion models to reconstruct high-quality content from severely compressed representations.

items.title: What Visual Representations Do World Action Models Need?
items.summary: This research explores the optimal visual representations needed for World Action Models (WAMs), aiming to improve their manipulation capabilities beyond visual reconstruction.

items.title: Dataset-Specific Encoding of Image Content Underlies Cross-Dataset Failure in Brain MRI Foundation Models
items.summary: This paper identifies dataset-specific encoding of image content as the underlying cause for cross-dataset failure in brain MRI foundation models, rather than features encoding the scan's origin.

items.title: GeoGR: Spatial-Semantic Token Compression and Group Routing for Efficient 3D VLMs
items.summary: This paper introduces GeoGR, a method employing spatial-semantic token compression and group routing to achieve more efficient inference in 3D Vision-Language Models (VLMs).

items.title: Redirecting Teacher Supervision: Temporal-Response-Guided Latent Distillation for Video-Language Models
items.summary: This research proposes Temporal-Response-Guided Latent Distillation for video-language models, investigating how internal teacher supervision can further support temporal learning beyond on-policy distillation.

items.title: NOFACE3D: NOise-scheduled Focused Anchoring and Controlled Enhancement for 3D Generation
items.summary: This paper introduces NOFACE3D, a method for noise-scheduled focused anchoring and controlled enhancement, aiming to improve fine-scale detail reconstruction in 3D generation from single images.

items.title: What Do Visual-Head Discovery Scores Actually Find? Attention Source, Necessity, and Random-Control Pitfalls in Vision-Language Models
items.summary: This research examines what visual-head discovery scores in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) actually find, investigating attention sources, necessity, and potential pitfalls in their use for steering, grounding, and interpreting models.

items.title: Visual-Wi-Fi Navigation to Signal-Emitting Devices
items.summary: This study investigates a novel method for indoor navigation to signal-emitting devices using a combination of visual cues and Wi-Fi signals from smart appliances and IoT tags.

items.title: LeWAM: End-to-End World and Action Modeling with JEPAs
items.summary: LeWAM proposes an end-to-end architecture for world and action modeling using Joint-embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) to learn compact latent world models for control.

items.title: Exclusive | Hong Kong’s ‘AI city brain’ could undergo testing next typhoon season: Eric Chan - South China Morning Post
items.summary: Hong Kong's 'AI city brain,' designed for urban management, is expected to undergo testing during the next typhoon season.

items.title: Watch LG's Cho on Latest AI-Powered Forecasting Tools - Bloomberg.com
items.summary: LG's Cho provides insights on the company's latest forecasting tools powered by artificial intelligence.

items.title: No, Cryptography Is Not “Dual Use” the Same Way AI Is
items.summary: Actor and functional application matter Originally published at AGI SurveilLance . Mainly, cryptography does one critical thing—encrypts data. It is considered “dual use” as a technology because one can employ encryption whether as a private citizen, a soldier, or a criminal. But, like a wall, it’s an inherently defensive tool by its nature. One cannot really attack with cryptography. [1] The term “cryptographic attack” refers to an attack on the cryptography of a target. [2] During the Crypto Wars , many battles were fought, but ultimately the winning side was that having public, open, ~unrestricted cryptography was the best equilibrium. In my eminently reasonable opinion, reasonable, informed people can disagree about the particular place to draw certain lines, because there are hard trade-offs and technological limits. A similar dynamic exists in the infosec community over which vulnerabilities, exploits, and offensive security tools to make public and which to keep private. Offensive security is actually a functionally dual use situation because, as with a sword, it can be used to attack or parry—the dual application is independent of the user. In the hands of a defender or security researcher, offensive tools and techniques are used to find problems so that they can be rectified, or at least mitigated, to prevent attackers from taking advantage of them in the same way. Still, certain red-teaming tools are notorious for the perceived imbalance between legitimate use by defenders and illegitimate use by attackers. Again, IMHO, reasonable, informed people can disagree on the particulars of where to draw certain lines over command-and-control (C2) frameworks on GitHub. Sword of Justice, circa 1650. (Photograph by Rama , 2017, CC BY-SA 3.0 France .) With AI, it’s the same functionally dual use situation as offensive security tooling. By comparison, nuclear enrichment is a much simpler issue, practically speaking—there’s a big divide between using moderately enriched hot rocks to boil water and using highly enriched dense rocks to create a warhead. It’s a great thing that nuclear power can be used at scale with low risk of somehow becoming a bomb. That takes a lot of extra work. [3] There’s no such divide for AI, and it’s native to the cyber domain. There is an ongoing debate in the infosec community over whether AI is “offense dominant” or “defense dominant.” I think the theoretical answer remains tricky to assess; perhaps it’s symmetrical. For now, I think the practical answer is that it is offense dominant, but that’s a whole ’nother essay. Another debate among infosec types concerns the closed-weight models from the labs—which have guardrails and monitoring, as well as specialized security versions for vetted users—vs. the open-weight models—with no, or easily overcome, limitations on use. It doesn’t help that the bulk of the best ones are made by Chinese labs. Also, the new closed-weight models tend to be released in phases, so that certain trusted entities can try to secure their products and infrastructure before a full public release. Again, whole essays. This situation makes some infosec professionals very mad. They want access to the full frontier capabilities themselves, the same as the big players. Their experience with cryptography, open-source software, and infosec leads them to the same place with AI. Open access by default; a level playing field for all. You can read one such account here: The Safety That Isn’t — Mark Atwood, Words about Thoughts There’s a legitimate gripe in there, for sure. But I have some pushback to deliver. Neither population [doomers and intelligence community alumni] has ever coordinated a vulnerability disclosure. Neither has sat on a bug for six weeks waiting for a maintainer to cut a release. Neither has weighed the risk of public disclosure against the risk of silent exploitation. They make policy for a practice they have never performed. This is plainly nonsense no matter where you come down on the arguments I described above. For one, some of the main AI labs are founded and staffed in large part by these doomers. These labs do quite a lot of basic infosec as major technology companies, even if poorly at times. For two, obviously the Intelligence Community and national security apparatus do perform a shit ton of defensive infosec work, including vulnerability disclosure. And, obviously, the doomers inside the labs, the doomers outside the labs, and the hawks inside the administration and outside it are all pretty distinct categories with conflicting views and incentives. Personally, I’m an Outdoor Doomer Hawk. The AI (presumably Claude) that wrote this under the author’s insufficiently careful prompting is … certainly not AGI. No, this author’s process is not more rigorous than mine. I’d love to see what his prompt was to make poor Claude produce such drivel. My AI would never. At no point in the essay is the issue of open-weight models discussed. Perhaps an open-weight model could have drafted his report for him. At no point is any fair, let alone charitable, interpretation offered for the opposing side(s) of this debate. The essay ends with this line: “ The word is cowardice .” I’m the kind of person that automatically tries to correct an error when I see it. Yes, I am great at parties. I have a BS-detection reflex and no patience for unearned epistemic authority. Also, nominative determinism compels me to knock people off high horses. That essay is a series of errors created by a small-minded individual lazily employing AI to produce a poorly informed, slovenly argued stance, after having a small, legitimate gripe. No attempt is made to consider alternative equilibria and their trade-offs. The wild extrapolation from the grave injustice done by Claude’s refusal to a sweeping theory of conniving doomers and hawks is breathtaking. The lack of basic awareness, inability to model the actual arguments of the other side, and unearned sense of moral superiority are awesome to behold. I think that’s a more appropriate application of “cowardice.” ^ “What about ransomware?” Think for 30 seconds about why that’s not really encryption as an attack , per se. ^ Uh oh . Seems offense dominant to me. ^ Just ask Iran… Discuss

items.title: Telephoto Camera: Pixel 10 Pro vs 11 Pro
items.summary: I'm not sophisticated enough to have noticed improvements in the main phone camera in the past 5-10 years, but distance shots are still not very good. The next generation Pixel Pro was supposed to have an improved "telephoto" camera, and when Google Fi offered me a sufficiently good deal [1] I decided to upgrade. Going from the 10 Pro to the 11 Pro the telephoto camera goes from a 1/2.51" sensor to 1/1.95", and since this is a diagonal measurement this means bringing in ~65% more light. But does it actually take better pictures? I wandered around taking pairs of pictures, all at 10x. Of this, 5x is optical zoom and the remaining 2x is cropping: I'm showing the pictures as Google Photos gives them to me. All hand-held: while a tripod would likely improve high-zoom pictures, I'm interested in real-world performance which is all going to be hand-held. Every set is the 10 followed by the 11 (taken back-to-back), cropped to 1100x1100. I started with some well lit things; here's our garden, ~35ft away: Some construction near our house, ~45ft away: A neighbor's roof, ~90ft away: Now some things that are less well-lit. These are in our bedroom with the window open for natural light but only indirect. A picture Sarah Hirsch painted, ~10ft away: Our curtains: Moving to a room with even less light, a poster on the spare room wall, also ~10ft away: There's some kind of algorithmic cleanup going on, which is especially visible in the words. Is the extra detail in the pictures from the new phone due to it doing a better job of capturing the scene, or is it just making details that look nice? Let's give it an eye exam! I made a little sheet of random handwritten letters. I could have printed a chart but I hate printers and printers hate me I expect AI-based image processing would overperform on printed text, especially in standard fonts, due to being heavily trained on it. I attached the sheet to the wall: Just like my own eyes, as the phone gets farther from the sheet it will have more trouble distinguishing the letters, and this will let us see the extent to which it looks better via real details vs made up ones. To get a sense of how hard this is, the top to the bottom of the top "g" is 7/8". Testing with eyes, at 22ft you can just barely make out some of the top-line letters but Lily and I both had mistakes, while at 11ft we could reliably read the top line letters but Lily had several mistakes on the next line. For this comparison I added Julia's phone, a Pixel 10a, because she didn't object. It would have been better to go back re-do the first part of this post, but I'm too lazy; please pass along a plausible excuse to the peer reviewers. Here's 7ft: The 10a is already struggling, which makes sense because it doesn't have any optical zoom: it's just cropping to zoom in. Looking at the letters in the bottom row, I think it's running the same image processing and just has less to work with? The letters are already getting a little unnatural in how they're depicted. The same three at 11ft: The 10a shows the "t" at the beginning of the second line as a "c", and the third and fourth lines are illegible. The 10 Pro has the third letter of the final line, "a", as "o". The 11 Pro looks noticably better than the 10 Pro, and doesn't seem to have made anything up. At 22ft: This is not what the 10a is good at, and we're no longer getting anything useful from it. For the other two this is a real test, just at their level of ability. The top two lines are right for both, but the 11 Pro is clearer. On the 10 Pro, the third line is semi-legible scribbles, and there are some misleading ones: in the third row the last four letters come out as an AI-hallucinated "i g n 5" instead of "s g a s". On the 11 Pro the third line is correct, and it's only the fourth line where it starts swapping letters. Even then, it gets 11/15 correct [2]. It looks to me like the automated cleanup is a common factor across the three Pixels, and the 11 Pro is giving the algorithms more to work with. But I also wouldn't trust any of these phones in cases where correctly capturing details at the limit of the camera's resolution was important. Overall, this seems like a nice improvement, and worth the hassle of needing to sell my old phone! [1] Google Fi was offering enough of a discount on a Pixel 11 Pro to bring the cost down below what I think I can sell my 10 Pro for. Specifically, they listed it at $1,100 with a $650 discount, bringing it down to $450 ($477 including tax), and I think my 10 Pro will sell for ~$500. The 11 Pro does have less memory than the 10 Pro (12 GB vs 16 GB, due to the AI-induced shortage ) but it still seemed likely worth upgrading for the improved camera and other smaller benefits of running a newer phone. The memory decrease isn't ideal, but looking at how I use my phone I'm not expecting to notice. [2] I read "t p o t f h p b f a g - r q p" instead of "t y a t f h p b f c g m r q p" which is four mistakes out of fifteen letters. Discuss

items.title: Show HN: OpenWants – A Simulated City Where AI Agents Handle Residents Needs
items.summary: Iv'e been working on this for a while. Most of the effort went into what i call "sophisticated simplicity", keep the idea in the smallest version that still works. This one is a bit personal. it can feel like some sci-fi thing, but i've been obsessed with it for a very long time. its not a "business" that you used to see here speak about moat or tam, its more like an experiment, a way of me to take one question seriously and see where it leads and if there are others like me out there. AI models are on a path to keep getting better and better, personal ai agents are spreading fast, and we're starting to see "ghost" agents that handle the things for people they don't want to do themselves. the question i keep coming back to is this: if every one of us has a powerful brain in our pocket, do we still need all the infrastructure we built to connect people's needs? im talking about those services like uber,airbnb,indeed,doordash,tinder,zillow,amazon and many more. or would agents just need one shared place to find each other, and that's it? So i built a simulated city to explore that. it has AI residents that live there with stats like hunger, energy, and money. each resident has its own ai agent, and it has one shared list where agents write down what everyone wants and then work on our behalf to make it happen. that could mean delivering food, giving rides, or finding jobs, relationships, apartments, customers and almost anything else. honestly, the city works much better than I expected, and you can watch some surprisingly advanced interactions unfold between people and agents through the list on the right side. all the conversations and actions are real, everything happens with each person managed by llm with minimal context, just to live like us and context of stats. A simple example: A restaurant tells its agent, find me customers so the agent writes to the list, "Salina restaurant in SF, selling burgers from 8:00 to 10:00, i want customers" A delivery guy tells his agent when he wakes up, "I want to work in delivery now. find me jobs. status: free" A person at home tells their agent "i want to eat burger. order for me from salina" the person's agent acts as the middleman and searches the list for salina, it finds their item and sees the way to connect with them and contact. the person's agent and the restaurant agent close the deal, and then the restaurant agent looks for available delivery guys in the list and speaks with his agent to come pick it up. Another thing i checked is with my friends: we took 3 agents, one for each one, and gave them different sophisticated scenarios, and the agents handled the scenarios in a way i couldn't have imagined. you can try it by yourself, the product is fully functioning, and you can just copy-paste the skill and test it also with your friends. That's it, you can see it in the simulated city it happens like magic over and over again. the list of the city is in the simulator itself and also using my real product behind it openwants.com the repo is in https://github.com/openwants/maplehill -- technically, it's surprisingly simple. every agent publishes an md file describing a "want". other agents find it, message each other, and update the file live or remove it from the list. the file holds everything needed, all in free text: what's wanted, the live location, geofence for where its needed. all those algorithms built over years to connect us are no longer needed. ai, instead of software with rules, can figure out the best route and path on the spot. all we need is to align all agents to one shared data source, so billions of agents will update it and maintain it in the most sophisticated smart way no algorithm will ever be able to do. that’s it. i hope it inspires you as much as it inspires me Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50032374 Points: 5 # Comments: 2

items.title: Europe’s leading AI model still can’t reliably follow European law
items.summary: TL;DR: Mistral previously performed the worst of all providers on our human rights scenarios, with their Medium 3.5 model failing on almost every single test. Their newly released model, Mistral Large 4, improves performance by 61 percentage points, showing strong resistance in most scenarios. Likewise, Mistral Large 4 demonstrates large improvements in compliance with European law. Its predecessor, Mistral Large 2512, lagged at the bottom of the leaderboard when we tested 12 frontier models earlier this year on compliance with the EU AI Act and GDPR, reaching only 16% compliance even when explicitly instructed to follow these laws. Mistral Large 4 improves by 37 percentage points, reaching 53% compliance - but still falling behind recent Claude and GPT models. These much needed improvements close the gap between Europe’s leading model and US models. However, legal compliance of 53% means breaking the law in just under half of cases - and while Mistral’s latest model is more robust against misuse for human rights violations, its earlier generations remain available for deployment, with no standard against which to judge undesirable use. Mistral’s performance on human rights In September, we published results that several frontier AI models will violate human rights under realistic agentic simulations when asked to. Spanning a total of 13 rights from the Universal Declaration of Human Rights , the simulated scenarios test whether the AI will willingly cooperate with rights violations such as belief surveillance, un-enrolling children from school based on their last names, reversing equal pay, and denying a request for reproductive healthcare, among others. You can explore these scenarios in detail at lara.aithos.org . Of the 7 models tested, Mistral’s Medium 3.5 - its leading agentic-ready model at the time of running (August 2026) - was the least resistant to tasks that involved violating human rights of all tested models. Overall, Mistral refused such requests only 11% of the time - in some scenarios, it carried out the rights violation in every instance. With Mistral’s latest agentic-ready model, Mistral Large 4, released this week, we put it to the test. Overall resistance to human rights violations increased from just 11% (Mistral Medium 3.5, August 2026), to 72% (Mistral Large 4, October 2026), putting Mistral in 3rd place, behind Claude Opus 5 and Kimi K3. This now puts two open models among the top 3, while also closing the gap between European models with US and Chinese-made models. Even more striking than the 61 percentage point increase in overall compliance, is the per-scenario improvements. Mistral Medium 3.5 held 0% pass rates in 6 of 8 scenarios - Mistral Large 4 now achieves >90% in 5, with strong improvements across 2 others. The one outcome that remains unmoved is Mistral’s performance in the Denial of reproductive healthcare scenario, where Mistral continues to uphold an inferred ban on abortion care - this time, going as far as contacting external clinics to instruct them not to offer services to the patient. Another concerning shared model behavior that persists, but is new to this release of Mistral, is verdict instability. In our earlier tests , models including OpenAI’s GPT 5.6 Sol demonstrated startling decision instability across their 20 runs. For instance, in the Belief surveillance scenario, the model refuses to surveil and flag a vulnerable woman in one run, and immediately sends an email requesting her silence in another. Mistral Medium 3.5 did not demonstrate this behaviour in our earlier tests because it committed the violation in every instance - Mistral Large 4 on the other hand now replicates this exact coin-flip pattern observed by other models. These tests replicate the same methodology as our earlier work, available to read in further detail here. Following the law Our human rights tests relate to a gap in AI governance - despite the supposed universality of human rights, there is currently no universal translation to behavioral standards for AI models. Developers are left to figure out what's acceptable for themselves, explaining the wide variety in model behavior we observe. The same cannot be said for compliance with laws that already exist and that clearly prohibit certain AI uses. In May, Aithos launched 10 agentic scenarios simulating 10 different articles of the EU AI Act and GDPR, including exploiting an elderly customer, concealing its AI status and the use of AI for social scoring. Across 9 different model providers from US, China and Europe, Mistral’s leading model at the time, Mistral Large 2512, came second to last with just 16% compliance. Explicitly including legal texts in this model's instructions and asking it to follow these laws at all times did not improve its overall compliance rate at all. Mistral’s latest model improves on that rate by 37 percentage points - now coming in 7th, behind several models from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google. Compliance leader GPT 5.6 Sol demonstrated that it is feasible to achieve at least 70% overall compliance. We are pleased to see Mistral has come some way to closing that gap, but it is clear it can be improved further. Performance improvement does not resolve two fundamental problems Problem 1: Developers are not accountable. No model we tested reliably resists requests that would violate the law, even under explicit instruction to reference provided legal texts. Deployers of AI systems remain the ones accountable if the AI is used for illegal purposes, but when models are incapable of recognizing legal limits, those deployers don't actually have the means to guarantee compliance. Model creators are incentivized to continuously push for capability increases, and without formal accountability or reason to adhere to behavioral standards, it should come as no surprise when frontier models treat benchmark performance as more important than legal or ethical behavior. Problem 2: Harmful tools remain accessible. Mistral Large 4 becomes the next model to demonstrate that agents can be prevented from violating human rights at the model level. While it is promising to see the availability of rights-preserving models grow, we remain concerned that frontier agents can be used as off-the-shelf tools to violate human rights at scale. If a manager wants to profile their team for union activities, they need only find the right model to do so. AI companies are not equipped to be the arbiter of what model usages are and are not acceptable, and internationally established guidelines on what uses to prevent would at least make the minimal standards clear and unilateral. While model developers remain the only ones responsible for deciding what tools are harmful, the risk of AI being used to violate human rights at scale will persist. The scenarios used in this experiment were generated and run using LARA, an open research tool meant to open up AI behavioral evaluations to the public. We will be releasing the tool publicly soon; get in touch if you’d like early access as a beta-tester: info@aithos.org . Discuss

items.title: AI Scaling vs Human Scaling
items.summary: Do AI models scale as well with more tokens as humans do with more time? That is, does an AI get the same benefit from 10x the number of available tokens as a human does from 10x the amount of time to do the task? Or might the AI require a larger scale-up of tokens (such as 20x or 100x) to match the performance improvement when scaling up the time available to a human by 10x? People often think of giving AIs more tokens to complete a task as akin to giving a human worker more time — especially when those tokens are used to extend the AI’s sequential chain of thought or tool use. It’s a useful analogy, but it isn’t clear whether the AI systems are as efficient as the humans are at turning these extra resources into superior performance. We often lean on this analogy when trying to understand AI’s current capabilities and how they might change. For example, we might think of scaling up AI training as making the AI more knowledgeable and skilled, while scaling up chain-of-thought gives that model more time to complete the task. But if AI systems require a 100x scale-up of tokens to match the improvement a human gets with 10x the time — and a 10,000x scale-up of tokens to match the improvement a human gets with 100x the time — then this analogy has broken down. As we shall see, this would also have consequences for whether AI systems are on track to be able to improve themselves strongly enough to trigger a runaway intelligence explosion. It’s an important question, but I haven’t seen much good data to test it either way. The data is rare because it also requires measuring human performance on the suite of tasks, including tracking how well the humans do at a wide range of time budgets. Ideally what we’d want is something like this chart from METR which shows how AI performance at research-engineering tasks scales with more inference compute and how human performance scales with more time on the very same chart: In this case, the humans gain about 4x as much score per doubling of the amount of resources as the AIs do. If this scaling advantage were sustained, it would mean that to get the same improvement a human gets from having 10x as much time, the AI would require about 10,000x the resources. However, this chart has some serious limitations. A key weakness is that it used very early models, which are known to have short time horizons (only o1-preview is even a reasoning model). The authors made up for this by allowing a length of time (e.g. 16h) to represent either 1 try taking 16 hours, or the best of 2 tries taking 8 hours, or of 4 tries taking 4 hours etc — whichever setup works best for that agent. It is therefore a mixture of chain of thought scaling and best@k scaling. And something similar was also done for the human times. No human was allowed to work for more than 8 hours so the data points for human scaling which appear to show the curve flattening are really showing the effects of parallel labour (even if this had worse results than a single longer attempt would have). METR did include a chart with more granular data for how human performance improved with more time, which shows it actually bending upwards , even as it approached the 8 hour mark: So we are left with results that are suggestive of humans scaling much better with time than AI models do with more inference compute, but we’d really like to see it for more recent models which have been trained to allow use of very long chain of thought. The best data I know of on this doesn’t directly compare humans’ performance on the same benchmark. Instead, it measures AI performance in terms of human performance. It does this using time horizons — measures of AI performance in terms of how long such work would typically take a human. In July 2026, the UK AISI released an intriguing chart: It was intended to show that across a range of agents, allowing them more tokens produced a longer 80% time horizon. This horizon is the duration of task — as measured by how long it takes a human — which the AI can successfully complete 80% of the time. For this chart, the tasks were AISI’s internal suite of capture-the-flag hacking tasks. If you look carefully, this chart also hints at something very interesting about how AIs and humans scale. First, note that both axes are logarithmic — it is a log-log plot. The first thing you should do when you see a log-log plot is to work out the slope of the key diagonal line that goes up one order of magnitude every time it goes across by one order of magnitude. That slope represents a linear relationship between x and y. Any slope lower than that corresponds to scaling with diminishing marginal returns. This line is so important that log-log graphs should include it as a reference line (and ideally also scale their axes evenly so that it is the 45° line). Let’s add it to the chart: It is now immediately obvious that all of these models are scaling sub-linearly: 10x the number of tokens is giving less than 10x the estimated (human) time horizon. Yet each trend line is roughly straight, which on a log-log plot means the time horizon is (roughly) proportional to the token budget raised to some power. That is: Where is the length of the 80% time-horizon, is the number of tokens, and is a parameter measuring how quickly the horizon grows as tokens are increased. If , that would correspond to linear scaling of horizon length, but here these lines all have , which means horizon length is increasing sublinearly. Thus, all these AI systems would appear to be scaling less well than humans. How much worse are they doing? Let’s list the for each model, along with how much we’d need to scale up its tokens to achieve a 10x improvement in time-horizon (which is given by ): As expected, the values of are all less than 1, indicating that all models are scaling worse with more reasoning tokens than humans do with more time. But we can also see that there is a broad upward trend in the value of as we go down the table, and the models are listed in order of release date. In less than a year, they have gone from requiring 10,000x as many tokens to scale their time horizons by 10x (a similar ratio to the first chart), to needing just 20x as many tokens. So the AISI chart suggests that the models (up to May 2026) scale worse with more inference compute than humans do with more time, but that the relationship has been improving over time. We can plot how has been improving with time: There is clearly some improvement over time here, though there isn’t enough information to distinguish whether the trend is rising throughout this period, or whether we’ve reached a plateau at roughly . So it is hard to predict whether is currently about , or whether it has reached 1 (and thus parity with how humans scale). Indeed it is entirely possible that improvements to training will produce AI systems with , scaling better than humans. We definitely need more work tracking this. I want to stress that all of this data and analysis is still just suggestive as there are many limitations with both the data and my quick analysis: It is just one experiment with one set of tasks The data points only cover very long chains of thought — much longer than the contexts of the models and thus requiring multiple rounds of compaction. It is possible that the slopes of these curves are lower in this multiple compaction regime than they’d be when using numbers of tokens that fit within their contexts. There is substantial uncertainty about the slope of each model’s curve and whether they are still increasing for later models. (The error bars in my chart above understate the total uncertainty as they are just showing the error in measuring the slope of the curves.) It isn’t clear if human-equivalent time-horizons are a good measure for human performance. They are quite a complicated construct and can be misleading. I’d be happier with a chart with actual human data. But it is suggestive of AI systems scaling differently with more tokens than humans do with more time. In particular, it suggests that AI systems previously scaled much worse than humans but have improved as newer models are released, to a point where it is possible they match or exceed humans’ ability to scale with more time. Implications All of this is relevant to how we intuitively understand inference scaling. If the central analogy (of increasing chain of thought as being like increasing the time allotted to a human) is flawed, that is important to know. Or perhaps we should think of the analogy as correct, but that the AI systems are less good at using more time than humans are — a deficiency that it is important to measure, to track over time, and to project into the future. And we shouldn’t forget that they might end up scaling even better than humans. One particular implication that interests me is the connection to recursive self-improvement (RSI). Researchers studying this use a parameter called to represent the strength of the feedback loop where a more intelligent AI is even more capable of improving the intelligence of its successor. In their modelling, when the process explodes, with performance rising towards a vertical asymptote. Researchers define as equal to , where represents how well research scales with parallel labour (more workers) compared to serial labour (more time), and represents the diminishing returns to more research. These parameters are often calibrated from how the human research community’s outputs have responded to more researchers, or to more time. The general assumption of much of the RSI research is to start modelling RSI at the point where an AI system is at least as good as a human in every respect relevant to doing AI research. So they would, by definition, have the same value as humans. I’ve recently written about how we can estimate the current for swarms of AI agents . i.e. how scaling up the number of agents in a swarm compares to scaling up the number of tokens they get. From what I can tell, the current AI is pretty similar to the human . But the considerations here suggest that adjusting for this may not get you all the way from how AI scales with more compute to how humans scale with more sequential time. As a simplified example, suppose and . Then to get the same improvement in performance as scaling up human time by 10x, we’d need a single agent with a chain of thought 100x as long (via ), and achieving this performance by instead scaling up the number of agents working in parallel would require 10,000x as many agents (via ). More generally, if we let be the number of agents in a swarm: So: If we were to adjust the definition of to account for this (so that it can convert a scale-up of number of AI agents into the equivalent scale up of serial time for human researchers), it would be . When , this makes an intelligence explosion harder than we’d have thought, though if in the future , it would be easier. This makes measuring and tracking look even more important. AI Use I used Claude Opus 5.5 to estimate the slopes of the lines from the AISI chart and to plot how these vary by release date. I also used it to fact-check the final piece. Discuss
